items.note: A big fair is held at Udaypur each Mahāśivarātri, drawing thousands from neighbouring districts to the Śiva temple.
items.gloss: Every year on this day a big fair is held in Udaypur, in which thousands of people, even from neighbouring districts, come for the Shiva temple.

items.note: On Mahāśivarātri a long crowd headed to the temple; four hundred police were deployed for thousands of devotees, with the local heritage team on the ground.
items.gloss: From two kilometres earlier we saw a long throng advancing toward the temple. Four hundred policemen were specially deployed for the convenience and security of the thousands of devotees arriving until evening. Udaypur's heritage team was in the field with government officers.

items.note: Author's account of a newly found 'missile temple' amid shrubs, with scattered stones suggesting a large complex, perhaps a math, temple or commercial establishment.
items.gloss: We decided to go see, with our new guests, the new discovery of the 'missile temple', which Praveen Sharma had already sent us in photos. Priyanka went on to the high platform of that temple, imprisoned by thorny bushes, peered into the sanctum and returned cautiously. Deepak looked at the stones scattered over the whole complex from all sides. This must have been a splendid vast complex. Some math or temple or some commercial establishment.

items.note: The 'missile-like' temple stands on a seven-foot platform in a very narrow design, with a worn Gaṇeśa figure at the door; looks more like an ascetic's meditation place.
items.gloss: As if a missile were ready to be launched. Exactly like a craft ready for space travel. On a seven-foot-high platform this is a temple of a very narrow design, at whose door is a worn figure of Ganesha. It is so small and thin that inside it feels less like a temple and more like a meditation place of an ascetic. A place that seems prepared for the practice of an accomplished sadhaka. The outer design is as though prepared on a computer.

items.note: The missile-shaped temple stands amid ruins of a grand complex in the middle of the settlement; described as a golden page of some century far from Udayāditya.
items.gloss: In the middle of the settlement this missile-shaped temple stood still in waiting silence amid the ruins of some grand complex. Making your way past dense bushes, when you reach in front of it there is nothing but amazement. This is a place that must have its own different story to tell. A golden page of some century far from Udayaditya.

items.note: Archaeologist Narayan Vyas, from photographs, assesses the missile temple as sixteenth-century, implying temple building continued for centuries after Udayāditya.
items.gloss: The renowned archaeologist Narayan Vyas, seeing its photographs, has assessed that it is of the 16th century. That is, temple construction continued for centuries after Udayaditya, while Udaypur had in this period fallen victim to Islamic invaders.

items.note: Awareness from neighbouring Ganj Basoda: a group of youths roams around Udaypur and social worker Praveen Sharma documents ruins.
items.gloss: The biggest change this year is that aware people of Ganj Basoda have begun to look anew at this sad town in their neighbourhood. They have begun to enquire after its welfare. A group of youths wanders around Udaypur every second or third day. Everywhere Udaypur is giving some new information about itself. Social worker Praveen Sharma goes every day, sometimes to some ruin, sometimes some old house, sometimes some thicket, turning the pages of Udaypur's forgotten story.

items.note: INTACH convener Dr. Madanmohan Upadhyay and technical team have closely inspected Udaypur and plan a long camp.
items.gloss: Dr. Madanmohan Upadhyay, convener of the Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage (INTACH), has closely inspected Udaypur with his technical team. His team is going to hold a long camp. This is good news for Udaypur after several decades.

items.note: Author says this may be the first attention at this level since temple maintenance under Gharde Sahib in the Scindia period.
items.gloss: Perhaps for the first time at this level someone has knocked, after the temple maintenance done under Gharde Sahib's supervision in the time of the Scindia royal house.

items.note: Author says the findings of two and a half months expose the Archaeology Department's way of working.
items.gloss: But whatever has come out in the last two and a half months is going to expose the working style of the dull-witted government functionaries of the Archaeology Department. Here a treasure of history lay open, and they were filling the belly of papers with budget. The stigma of failing to save even the old, let alone find something new, is on their foreheads.

items.note: Author calls Udayāditya the 12th Paramāra king and Bhoja's brother, inferring he learned statecraft with Bhoja and was sent here as feudatory.

claim.value: brother of Bhoja (author's statement); 12th Paramāra king

items.gloss: King Udayaditya, after whom this town is named, is the 12th king of the Paramara dynasty. He is King Bhoja's brother. That is, he must have learned and understood the ways of governance along with King Bhoja, and when King Bhoja was overseeing his empire from the capital Dhar, Udayaditya must have been sent here as feudatory.

items.note: Udaypur lay on the Paramāra border; a fort-wall and hill fortification remnants and the large palace complex suggest royal kin guarded this frontier.
items.gloss: Udaypur was on the geographic border of the Paramara dynasty, which was strategically important. Remains of a fortification on the hill adjoining Udaypur, surrounded on all sides by a fort, are visible even on Google Map. Besides the main temple, the presence of the large palace complex shows that family members of the Paramara kings themselves must have been here for the security of this border.

items.note: Abundant stone let the Paramāras raise architectural masterpieces, competing with the Cholas, and build temples, palaces, tanks, stepwells and Sanskrit learning centres.
items.gloss: The abundant availability of stone gave the Paramara dynasty the opportunity to raise splendid specimens of architecture. In this work the Paramara kings competed as it were with the Chola kings of Tamil Nadu. Everywhere in their kingdom they had matchless temples, palaces, tanks, stepwells and centres of Sanskrit learning built.

items.note: Bhoja's 'Samarāṅgaṇa Sūtradhāra' testifies to his patronage of creativity; he built Sarasvatī Kaṇṭhābharaṇa centres at Ujjain, Māṇḍū and Dhār.
items.gloss: King Bhoja's treatise 'Samarangana Sutradhara' is evidence of what high level of creativity he patronised as a scholar. Among Paramara kings Bhoja's stature is like the sun shining among stars. He had Sarasvati Kanthabharana built in Ujjain, Mandu and Dhar, which were temples of Sarasvati and centres of learning in all branches of knowledge of the time including the Sanskrit language. Mandu was then known as Mandapadurga, and the name of the head of one hostel of the Sarasvati Kanthabharana there, Govinda Bhatta, is recorded in history.

items.note: Udayāditya, living at Udaypur, extended his glorious royal tradition and still glows in the region's memory.
items.gloss: Udayaditya, while living in Udaypur, carried forward his glorious royal tradition. That is why, even after centuries, he still glows in the memories of this entire region.

reject_reason: reflective essay on festivals and history; no citable evidence about Udaypur beyond one generic sentence

items.note: Narayan Vyas, posted to Udaypur at start of ASI service in 1972, recalls houses abutting the temple on three sides removed with compensation; clearing four feet of debris revealed the temple's foundation.
items.gloss: Dr. Narayan Vyas, who began his service in the Archaeological Survey of India in 1972 and was sent straight to Udaypur at the start of his job. He remembers well that then people had built their houses completely adjoining the temple on three sides. They were decades old. Then those people were removed after being given compensation. When four feet of debris was removed on all three sides, the splendid foundation of the temple came out, which can be seen even today.

items.note: Two houses in front were left and are still inhabited; the encroachment on the Nīlakaṇṭheśvara temple was not removed.
items.gloss: But two houses in front were left. People are living in them comfortably to this day. Perhaps the compensation seemed less to them. The deal may not have been settled. So they must have refused to move. This encroachment on the Nilakantheshwar Mahadev temple was not removed, and has not been.

reject_reason: biographical praise of Dr. Narayan Vyas and a Gujarat stepwell; no Udaypur evidence

items.note: Vyas says in 1972 the temple first called him to clean its surroundings; after independence and ASI taking the temple in, that was the first major visible work, and no one attended to Udaypur afterwards.
items.gloss: When he reached Udaypur he revealed that in 1972 Lord Nilakantheshwar had first called him for cleaning of his surroundings. Now he had come to see another big cleaning in Udaypur. After the ASI took the temple under its shelter after independence, that was the first major work that was visible. But after that, in so many years, no one took care of Udaypur.

items.note: Udaypur has four state-government monuments on which funds were regularly spent, though no one asked what the place actually needed.
items.gloss: There are four monuments of the state government in Udaypur, on which the funds that came continued to be spent. The belly of papers kept being filled. But no one took the trouble to ask Udaypur about its real needs.

items.note: The four state-protected monuments: two mosques (age garbled in OCR, about three hundred years), the Pisanhārī temple and a 27-foot Naṭarāja Śiva figure on the Rāvaṇaṭol rock.
items.gloss: Among the four protected monuments, two mosques, about three hundred years old, are also in the state government's charge. Of the remaining two, one is Pisanhari's temple and the other is the 27-foot-long statue of Nataraja Shiva built on the rock of Ravanatol.

items.note: Author states MP government spent Rs 1.10 crore in Udaypur in five years; later sentences (author's source: an official) say Rs 67 lakh went to one mosque.
items.gloss: In Udaypur the Madhya Pradesh government spent one crore ten lakh rupees in the last five years.

items.note: An official cited by the author says the largest share, 67 lakh of the 1.10 crore, went to one mosque while thousand-year-old palaces were left abandoned.
items.gloss: An officer who looked at the budget files told me that out of one crore ten lakh, the most, 67 lakh rupees, was spent on one mosque alone, while thousand-year-old palaces were left completely abandoned to ruin. Remains of many broken temples were lying scattered around Udaypur beyond count.

items.note: Locals have always called one of the two mosques the 'kachahri'; a signboard once said so; its conversion to a mosque is unknown, now the Jāmā Masjid remembered with Jahāngīr's name.
items.gloss: One of the two mosques Udaypur people have called the 'kachahri' since childhood; their forefathers too had told them it is the kachahri. People remember that a signboard named kachahri was once also put up. When a kachahri was turned into a mosque, no one knows. Not just a mosque, the Jama Masjid. It is remembered by the name of Emperor Jahangir.

items.note: Funds came for four monuments, with more than half going to one monument, and nobody visited to see why.
items.gloss: Funds came for four monuments. But looking toward the fifth and sixth and including them in the list was a task beyond closed-minded government functionaries. Before releasing funds no one thought it proper to come to Udaypur and see: if more than half the amount is being consumed on one monument alone, what is its speciality and to whom and why is it visible?

items.note: Author's imaginative reading of the structure as a court hall for king, ministers and craftsmen; mentions guidance on building the Uday Samudra (speculation).
items.gloss: This is a structure like a Darbar-e-Aam or Darbar-e-Khas, where the king or emperor must have sat with his ministers, guests or notables of the city. People must have come to them with their problems and information. They must have sat with their engineers and architects to understand every detail of temple construction and discussed financial matters. In the next audience he must have addressed the group of craftsmen who came for guidance on the construction of Uday Samudra and given information on the construction of the Sabha Mandal in Bhopal.

items.note: Author says the kachahri / Jāmā Masjid was clearly a part of the Paramāra-era palace, on the palace's right in a four-bigha courtyard with four bastions and twenty-foot walls.
items.gloss: The special point is that this kachahri, or Jama Masjid of the Muslim brothers, has clearly been a part of the palace of Paramara times, which was once to the right of the palace in a spacious four-bigha courtyard surrounded by four bastions and twenty-foot-high walls.

items.note: A farman enjoining prayer-offerers to remember Bābur with the fātiḥā was presented as proof of ownership of the palace.
items.gloss: And this is the same mosque where a decree recorded the order for those who offer namaz to remember Hazrat Firoz Makani Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur with the Fatiha prayer, which was presented as proof of ownership over the palace.

reject_reason: political polemic about Mughal period and Congress; no citable evidence on Udaypur
political polemic about heritage funding; no citable evidence on Udaypur

items.note: Author says Rāvaṇaṭol and Pisanhārī are neglected and ASI staff cannot guide visitors to Udaypur's other sites.
items.gloss: Ravanatol and Pisanhari are also only a neglected part of Udaypur's suppressed past. Most people coming from outside have no one to tell them anything about them. ASI employees are completely failing to tell visitors to the temple about the other things of this town. Whatever their jobs, they could at least have been made capable of advising visitors to the temple to visit the four best places of Udaypur, or at least telling ten minutes of facts about the temple.

items.note: Proposal: a Sunday heritage walk with printed material for visitors, a cheap undertaking authorities could support.
items.gloss: Printed material could also have been prepared to attract tourists on a declared memorable heritage walk every Sunday. In this very cheap and low-budget work the Centre, the state government, the District Archaeology Association or the local panchayat could have lent a hand.

items.note: Author says the Vidisha District Archaeology Association meets every couple of years; its last meeting was a year and a half earlier with unknown outcome.
items.gloss: The meeting of the District Archaeology Association at Vidisha district headquarters has been ending every two-four years as a comfortable session of joking with officers over tea and coffee. I learnt that the association's last meeting in Vidisha was a year and a half ago. Who knows why they sat, and no one knows what came out of that meeting.

items.note: Author attributes neglect of heritage to governments' indifference since the start, across parties.
items.gloss: This is the bad result of the government's feeble attitude toward history, archaeology and culture from the very beginning. The crop of awareness could not wave from seeds of neglect. This same attitude of Congress governments was responsible for the slow destruction of our heritage, and the later Janata Party and Bharatiya Janata Party governments were also no angels. This blindness toward heritage was equal on both sides.

items.note: Author proposes that schools and colleges bring every child to such sites, with questions answered and documented history told.
items.gloss: To break our unconcern, our coming here again and again should have been made compulsory. Every school and college should have been bound to bring each of its children here continuously, and asking questions should be compulsory. Their questions should be answered and the history of this place told. History means not half-baked truth but full and real history. What was there before and what happened later should be told to them in full detail with documentary evidence.

items.note: Bījā Maṇḍal at Vidisha: its height given as 105 gaz by Minhāj Sirāj in the Tabaqāt-i-Nāṣirī, the only Delhi chronicler to record the destruction by Iltutmish; Paramāra king Devapāla Deva's troops at the Vidisha fort.
items.gloss: Seeing those broken stones of the Bija Mandal in Vidisha you can imagine that it must have been one of the biggest temples in the country in its time. Its height of 105 gaz was written by Minhaj Siraj in the 'Tabaqat-i-Nasiri', the only Delhi chronicler recording the devastation of Iltutmish's attack. When the soldiers of the Paramara king Devapala Deva posted at Vidisha's fort were defeated, those Islamic plunderers must have entered the city, and the Vijay temple visible from miles away must have been seized first in groups.
